sub_terms.definition: A branching tree diagram that shows how species are related through evolution — the closer two species are on the tree, the more recently they shared an ancestor.

student_glossary.definition: Where species are found around the world. The patterns don't match habitat alone — they match evolutionary history. Species on islands tend to resemble nearby mainland species, not species in similar habitats far away.
student_glossary.example: Australia has kangaroos and koalas but Africa doesn't — not because Africa lacks suitable habitat, but because marsupials evolved and diversified in Australia after it separated from other continents.

student_glossary.definition: The process by which one species gradually splits into two or more separate species over many generations, usually when populations are separated and face different selection pressures.
student_glossary.example: A river divides a mouse population — over thousands of generations, the two groups face different predators and food sources, accumulate different traits, and eventually can no longer interbreed. Two species now exist where one used to.

sub_terms.definition: When a physical barrier (mountain range, ocean, river) separates a population so the groups can't interbreed — a common first step toward speciation.
sub_terms.example: When a land bridge floods, island populations can no longer mix with mainland populations — each group then evolves independently.

sub_terms.definition: When one species rapidly diversifies into many new species, each filling a different ecological role — like Darwin's finches evolving different beak shapes for different food sources on the Galápagos Islands.

student_glossary.definition: When every individual of a species dies and the species is gone permanently. This happens when the environment changes faster than the population can adapt through natural selection.
student_glossary.example: Dinosaurs dominated Earth for over 160 million years but went extinct after an asteroid strike rapidly changed conditions — they weren't 'bad at surviving,' the environment just changed too fast for natural selection to keep up.

sub_terms.definition: A catastrophic event that wipes out a huge proportion of all species in a short time — five major ones have happened in Earth's history.
sub_terms.example: The mass extinction 66 million years ago killed about 75% of all species, including the dinosaurs — but mammals survived and diversified into the niches left empty.

student_glossary.definition: The variety of different species in an area or on Earth as a whole. Biodiversity isn't random — it's the result of billions of years of evolution, speciation, and extinction. It's still changing today as species evolve and face new pressures.
student_glossary.example: The Amazon rainforest has enormous biodiversity because millions of years of evolution in a stable, resource-rich environment produced many specialised species — but deforestation is now a selection pressure that threatens this diversity.

student_glossary.definition: The distance that light travels in one year — about 9.46 trillion kilometres. Despite having 'year' in the name, it's a unit of distance, not time. It's used because space is so enormous that kilometres would give numbers too large to be useful.
student_glossary.example: The nearest star to our Sun is about 4.2 light-years away — meaning the light you see from it tonight actually left that star 4.2 years ago.

sub_terms.definition: The distance from Earth to the Sun — about 150 million km. Used for distances within our solar system where light-years would be too large.
sub_terms.example: Mars is about 1.5 AU from the Sun — one and a half times the Earth-Sun distance.

sub_terms.definition: A shorthand for writing really big or really small numbers using powers of ten — for example, 9,460,000,000,000 km becomes 9.46 × 10¹² km.
sub_terms.example: Writing the distance to the nearest star as 40,000,000,000,000 km is unwieldy — 4.0 × 10¹³ km says the same thing much more clearly.

student_glossary.definition: A massive collection of billions of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. Our galaxy (the Milky Way) is just one of billions of galaxies in the observable universe.
student_glossary.example: The Milky Way contains roughly 200 billion stars — and the observable universe contains roughly 200 billion galaxies, each with billions of their own stars.

sub_terms.definition: The part of the universe we can actually see — limited by how far light has been able to travel since the big bang. The real universe may be much bigger than what we can observe.
sub_terms.example: It's like standing in a fog — you can only see so far, but the world doesn't end where your vision stops. The observable universe is our 'vision limit' set by the speed of light.

student_glossary.definition: The scientific model that explains how the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. All space, time and matter started from an incredibly hot, dense state and the universe has been expanding and cooling ever since. It's not an explosion in space — space itself has been stretching.
student_glossary.example: Imagine dots drawn on a balloon being inflated — every dot moves away from every other dot as the balloon stretches. The universe works the same way: galaxies aren't flying through space, the space between them is expanding.

sub_terms.definition: The ongoing stretching of space itself, causing galaxies to move further apart over time — confirmed by the observation that distant galaxies are redshifted.
sub_terms.example: Space between galaxies is literally getting bigger — like a rubber band being stretched with ants on it. The ants aren't walking apart; the rubber between them is growing.

sub_terms.definition: An invisible form of matter that doesn't give off or absorb light — we know it exists because of its gravitational effects, but scientists don't yet know what it's made of.
A mysterious form of energy that seems to be making the universe's expansion speed up — it makes up about 68% of the universe but is one of science's biggest unsolved questions.
The starting point of the big bang — an incredibly hot, dense state where everything was compressed into an unimaginably small point. It's the 'time zero' of the universe's timeline.

student_glossary.definition: When light from a distant galaxy is stretched to longer wavelengths (shifted toward the red end of the spectrum) because the galaxy is moving away from us or because space is expanding. The galaxy doesn't emit red light — its light gets stretched during the journey.
student_glossary.example: A galaxy 1 billion light-years away has its light stretched more than one 100 million light-years away — the further away, the more the light is redshifted, showing that more distant galaxies are receding faster.

sub_terms.definition: Edwin Hubble discovered that the further away a galaxy is, the more its light is redshifted — proving the universe is expanding.
sub_terms.example: Hubble plotted galaxy distance against redshift and found a straight-line relationship — the pattern is exactly what you'd expect if space is expanding everywhere.

sub_terms.definition: The opposite of redshift — when light is squeezed to shorter wavelengths because a galaxy is moving toward us.
sub_terms.example: The Andromeda galaxy is blue-shifted because it's close enough to be pulled toward us by gravity, overriding the general expansion.

sub_terms.definition: The distance between peaks of a wave. For light, shorter wavelengths look blue and longer wavelengths look red.

student_glossary.definition: The change in wavelength you observe when a source of waves is moving toward or away from you. The same thing that makes an ambulance siren sound higher-pitched as it approaches and lower-pitched as it drives away also applies to light from galaxies.
student_glossary.example: An ambulance siren sounds high-pitched coming toward you (waves compressed) and low-pitched moving away (waves stretched) — galaxy light works the same way, stretching redder when the galaxy moves away.

student_glossary.definition: A faint glow of microwave radiation that fills the entire universe — the leftover heat from when the universe was incredibly hot and dense shortly after the big bang. The big bang theory predicted this glow should exist, and scientists detected it in 1965.
student_glossary.example: If you tuned an old analogue TV between channels, about 1% of the static you'd see comes from the CMB — you'd literally be looking at the afterglow of the big bang.

student_glossary.definition: The process that created the lightest elements — mostly hydrogen and helium — in the first few minutes after the big bang, when the universe was hot enough for nuclear reactions. The big bang model predicts roughly 75% hydrogen and 25% helium, and that's what we actually observe.
student_glossary.example: Almost all the hydrogen in the water you drink was made in the first few minutes after the big bang — heavier elements like carbon and iron were made much later, inside stars.

student_glossary.definition: Energy from the Sun, mostly as visible light. When it reaches Earth, some is absorbed by the surface (warming it up) and some is reflected back to space. How much gets absorbed depends on what the surface looks like.
student_glossary.example: A dark asphalt road absorbs most sunlight and gets very hot, while fresh snow reflects most of it and stays cold — different surfaces absorb different amounts of solar energy.

sub_terms.definition: How reflective a surface is. Ice and snow have high albedo (reflect a lot); oceans and dark soil have low albedo (absorb a lot).
sub_terms.example: When Arctic ice melts and exposes dark ocean water, the albedo drops — more energy is absorbed, causing even more warming, which melts more ice.

student_glossary.definition: The balance between energy coming into Earth's system from the Sun and energy going out as infrared radiation. When these are equal, Earth's temperature stays stable. When more energy comes in than goes out, the planet warms up.
student_glossary.example: Think of a bathtub with the tap on and the drain open — if water flows in as fast as it flows out, the level stays the same. If you partly block the drain (like adding greenhouse gases), water (energy) builds up.

sub_terms.definition: The solid Earth — rocks, soil and landforms.
All living things and ecosystems on Earth.
All the water on Earth — oceans, rivers, lakes and ice.
The layer of gases surrounding Earth, including the greenhouse gases that trap heat.
Large-scale flows of water that move heat around the planet — warm currents carry tropical heat toward the poles, helping regulate climate in different regions.

student_glossary.definition: The process where greenhouse gases in the atmosphere trap heat that Earth's surface is trying to radiate back to space. The surface absorbs sunlight, warms up, and emits infrared radiation — greenhouse gases catch some of that infrared and send it back down, keeping Earth warmer than it would be without an atmosphere.
student_glossary.example: Without any greenhouse effect, Earth's average temperature would be about −18°C — far too cold for life as we know it. The natural greenhouse effect keeps it at about +15°C.

sub_terms.definition: The type of energy that warm objects give off — you can't see it, but you can feel it as heat. Earth's surface emits infrared radiation, and this is what greenhouse gases trap.
sub_terms.example: Hold your hand near (not on) a hot pavement on a summer evening — the warmth you feel is infrared radiation being emitted by the surface.

sub_terms.definition: The normal, baseline greenhouse warming that has kept Earth habitable for billions of years — this is a good thing.
The extra warming caused by humans adding more greenhouse gases to the atmosphere — this is what's driving current climate change.
sub_terms.example: Burning coal and oil releases CO₂ that had been locked underground for millions of years — this extra CO₂ traps more infrared radiation than the natural level would.

student_glossary.definition: A gas in the atmosphere that absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation, contributing to the greenhouse effect. The main ones are carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), water vapour and nitrous oxide (N₂O).
student_glossary.example: CO₂ from burning petrol in your car enters the atmosphere, where it absorbs infrared radiation that Earth was trying to send back to space — trapping that energy in the climate system.

sub_terms.definition: The main greenhouse gas from burning fossil fuels — it stays in the atmosphere for centuries.
A greenhouse gas much more powerful than CO₂ per molecule but shorter-lived — released by livestock, rice paddies, landfills and gas leaks.

student_glossary.definition: When more energy enters Earth's system than leaves it — like turning up the tap in a bathtub without opening the drain wider. The extra greenhouse gases trap more outgoing infrared radiation, creating a surplus of energy that warms the planet.
student_glossary.example: Right now, Earth is absorbing about 1 watt per square metre more than it's emitting — that doesn't sound like much, but across the entire planet it adds up to enormous amounts of extra heat.

student_glossary.definition: When the result of a process feeds back to make that process stronger (positive feedback) or weaker (negative feedback). In climate, positive feedbacks mean a small initial warming can trigger changes that cause even more warming.
student_glossary.example: Warming melts ice → darker ocean absorbs more heat → more warming → more ice melts — each step makes the next one worse. That's a positive feedback loop.

sub_terms.definition: Warming causes more water to evaporate, and water vapour is itself a greenhouse gas — so more evaporation means more greenhouse warming, which causes more evaporation.

student_glossary.definition: A measurable sign that the climate is changing — not just temperature, but also sea level, ice coverage, species ranges, ocean acidity and more. Different indicators show up in different parts of the Earth system.
student_glossary.example: Rising sea levels, shrinking Arctic ice, coral bleaching and birds nesting earlier in spring are all climate change indicators — they're different measurements showing the same underlying energy imbalance.

sub_terms.definition: A feedback loop where melting ice (which reflects sunlight) exposes darker surfaces (which absorb it), causing more warming, which melts more ice.
Ground that stays frozen year-round in polar regions. When it thaws, it releases stored CO₂ and methane, adding more greenhouse gas and creating another feedback loop.
sub_terms.example: Siberian permafrost has been frozen for thousands of years — as it thaws, the ancient plant material trapped inside decomposes and releases greenhouse gases.

student_glossary.definition: The global increase in average sea level, caused by two things: ocean water expanding as it warms (thermal expansion) and extra water from melting glaciers and ice sheets. Both are driven by the same energy imbalance.
student_glossary.example: Even if no ice melted at all, sea level would still rise just from the ocean water expanding as it gets warmer — that accounts for roughly half of the rise we've seen so far.

sub_terms.definition: When water gets warmer, it takes up more space. The ocean is absorbing most of the extra heat from the energy imbalance, so it's expanding — raising sea levels.

student_glossary.definition: Actions that tackle the cause of climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions or removing greenhouse gases from the atmosphere — fixing the energy imbalance itself, not just dealing with its effects.
student_glossary.example: Replacing a coal power plant with a solar farm is mitigation — it reduces CO₂ emissions going into the atmosphere, directly addressing the cause of the energy imbalance.

student_glossary.definition: Actions that help people and ecosystems cope with the effects of climate change that are already happening or unavoidable — adjusting to consequences rather than fixing the cause.
student_glossary.example: Building higher sea walls to protect a coastal city from rising sea levels is adaptation — it doesn't stop the sea from rising, but it protects the city from the effects.

student_glossary.definition: A push or pull on an object. Every force has a size (how strong) and a direction (which way), so you always draw it as an arrow. Forces can act by touching (friction, pushing) or without touching (gravity).
student_glossary.example: When you kick a ball, your foot applies a contact force — the arrow points in the direction you kicked, and the length shows how hard.

student_glossary.definition: A quantity that has both a size and a direction. Force, velocity and acceleration are all vectors — you need to know which way they point, not just how big they are.
student_glossary.example: Saying 'the wind is 30 km/h' only tells you speed; saying 'the wind is 30 km/h from the north' gives you the full vector because it includes direction.

sub_terms.definition: The size or amount of something — just the number, without direction. Speed is the magnitude of velocity (e.g. 60 km/h, no direction specified).
Which way a force or motion acts — it's what makes velocity different from speed. 60 km/h north is a velocity (has direction); 60 km/h is just speed (no direction).
A quantity with only size, no direction — like mass, speed or temperature.
A rule you set at the start of a problem to decide which direction is positive and which is negative.

student_glossary.definition: The overall force on an object when you add up all the individual forces, taking direction into account. If forces push in opposite directions, they partly or fully cancel each other out.
student_glossary.example: If you push a box with 20 N to the right and friction pushes back with 5 N to the left, the net force is 15 N to the right.

student_glossary.definition: A force between two surfaces that opposes motion — it always pushes against the direction an object is moving or trying to move. Friction is why things slow down and stop even when you stop pushing them.
student_glossary.example: A ball rolled across carpet stops quickly because of high friction; the same ball on polished floorboards keeps rolling much longer because there is less friction.

student_glossary.definition: An object stays still or keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction unless a net force acts on it. This means you don't need a force to keep something moving — you only need a force to change its motion.
student_glossary.example: A hockey puck on ice slides a long way because there is very little friction — without that opposing force, it would keep going forever.

sub_terms.definition: An object's tendency to resist any change in its motion — heavier objects have more inertia, which is why they are harder to start moving or stop.
sub_terms.example: It's much harder to push a loaded shopping trolley than an empty one because the loaded trolley has more inertia.

student_glossary.definition: Moving at the same speed in the same direction with no acceleration and no net force. An object at constant velocity is not speeding up or slowing down — it is in a state where all forces are balanced.
student_glossary.example: A car cruising on a straight highway at a steady 100 km/h has constant velocity — the engine force exactly balances air resistance and friction, so the net force is zero.

student_glossary.definition: How quickly velocity changes, calculated by dividing the change in velocity by the time taken (a = Δv/t). Acceleration isn't just speeding up — slowing down and changing direction also count as acceleration because the velocity is changing.
student_glossary.example: A car going from 0 to 60 km/h in 10 seconds is accelerating. A car braking from 60 to 0 is also accelerating — just in the opposite direction to its motion.

sub_terms.definition: Acceleration in the opposite direction to motion, which causes an object to slow down. It's not a separate thing — it's just acceleration with a negative sign.
sub_terms.example: When a car brakes, the deceleration is caused by the friction force from the brakes opposing the car's forward motion.

sub_terms.definition: A graph that shows how an object's velocity changes over time. The steepness (gradient) of the line tells you the acceleration — a flat line means constant velocity, not zero velocity.
sub_terms.example: A straight line sloping upward on a velocity-time graph means steady acceleration — the object is speeding up at a constant rate.

sub_terms.definition: A graph showing how far an object has travelled over time. A straight line means constant speed; a curve means the speed is changing.

student_glossary.definition: Speed with a direction attached. Two objects can have the same speed but different velocities if they are moving in different directions. Changing direction — even at the same speed — counts as a change in velocity.
student_glossary.example: A car doing 60 km/h north and a car doing 60 km/h south have the same speed but opposite velocities.

sub_terms.definition: How fast something is moving, without caring about direction.

student_glossary.definition: The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration: F = ma. This means a bigger force causes more acceleration, and a heavier object needs more force to accelerate the same amount.
student_glossary.example: Pushing an empty shopping trolley with a certain force makes it accelerate quickly; the same push on a full trolley gives less acceleration because the mass is greater.

sub_terms.definition: The unit used to measure force — 1 newton is the force needed to accelerate 1 kilogram at 1 m/s².
When one quantity changes, the other changes by the same factor — double the force means double the acceleration (if mass stays the same).
sub_terms.example: If 10 N gives an acceleration of 2 m/s², then 20 N gives 4 m/s² — the acceleration doubled because the force doubled.

student_glossary.definition: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. Mass stays the same no matter where you are — unlike weight, which changes depending on gravity.
student_glossary.example: An astronaut has the same mass on the Moon as on Earth (say, 70 kg), but their weight on the Moon is only about one-sixth of their weight on Earth because the Moon's gravity is weaker.

sub_terms.definition: The force of gravity pulling on an object, measured in newtons. Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = mg).
sub_terms.example: A 70 kg person weighs about 686 N on Earth (70 × 9.8) but only about 114 N on the Moon.

student_glossary.definition: Whenever one object pushes or pulls another, the second object pushes or pulls back with the same size force in the opposite direction. These two forces always act on different objects — that's why they don't cancel each other out.
student_glossary.example: When you jump, your feet push down on the ground and the ground pushes up on you with an equal force — it's the ground's push that launches you upward.

sub_terms.definition: The two equal-and-opposite forces that arise from an interaction between two objects — one force on each object.
sub_terms.example: A swimmer pushes water backward with their hands (action); the water pushes the swimmer forward (reaction).

student_glossary.definition: When all the forces on a single object add up to zero, so the object doesn't accelerate. This is different from Newton's Third Law pairs, which act on two different objects.
student_glossary.example: A book sitting on a table has balanced forces — gravity pulls it down and the table pushes it up with equal force, so it stays still.

student_glossary.definition: A simple drawing of one object showing all the forces acting on it as labelled arrows. You draw the object as a dot or box and add every force — gravity, friction, normal force, any push or pull — before doing any calculations.
student_glossary.example: For a box being pushed across a floor, your free body diagram would show four arrows: weight downward, normal force upward, applied force forward, and friction backward.

student_glossary.definition: The support force a surface pushes back with when an object sits on or presses against it. It acts at right angles to the surface. On a flat floor, the normal force pushes straight up.
student_glossary.example: Right now, the chair you are sitting on is pushing up on you with a normal force — if it didn't, you would fall through it.

student_glossary.definition: Design features in cars — crumple zones, airbags, seatbelts — that protect people in a crash by spreading out the stopping time. A longer stopping time means a smaller force on your body, because the same speed change happens more gradually.
student_glossary.example: A crumple zone at the front of a car crumples slowly during a crash, giving the car (and you) more time to stop — so the force on you is much less than hitting a rigid wall.

student_glossary.definition: The total distance a car travels from when the driver sees a hazard to when it fully stops. It has two parts: the distance you travel while your brain reacts (reaction distance), plus the distance while the brakes slow you down (braking distance). Both get longer at higher speeds, but braking distance grows much faster.
student_glossary.example: At 60 km/h you might stop in about 45 metres total, but at 80 km/h it's not just a bit more — it's roughly 73 metres. The braking distance grows with speed squared, which is why small speed increases make a big difference.

student_glossary.definition: A First Nations Australian tool (also called a woomera) that makes a spear's arm effectively longer, so force is applied over a greater distance and time. This gives the spear more speed and hitting power — Newton's Second Law in action.
student_glossary.example: A spearthrower lets a hunter launch a spear much faster than a hand throw alone, because the force acts over a longer distance, giving the spear more time to accelerate.

student_glossary.definition: A diagram of an atom showing electrons arranged in rings (shells) around the nucleus. Each shell can hold a set number of electrons: the first holds 2, the second holds 8, and the third holds 8. You fill from the inside out.
student_glossary.example: Sodium (Na, 11 electrons) is drawn as 2 electrons in the first shell, 8 in the second, and 1 in the third — that single outer electron is what makes sodium so reactive.

sub_terms.definition: A ring around the nucleus where electrons sit. Inner shells fill first, and each has a maximum capacity.
How many electrons each shell can hold — 2 in the first, 8 in the second, 8 in the third.

student_glossary.definition: The electrons in the outermost shell of an atom — not the total number of electrons, just the ones in the last ring. This number is the key to understanding an element's chemical behaviour and where it sits in the periodic table.
student_glossary.example: Carbon has 6 electrons total (2 in the first shell, 4 in the second) — its 4 outer-shell electrons determine how it bonds, not the total of 6.

sub_terms.definition: How many bonds an atom can form, based on how many outer-shell electrons it can lose, gain or share.

student_glossary.definition: The unique pattern of coloured lines an element produces when its atoms are given energy (like in a flame). Each element has its own pattern because its electrons jump between specific energy levels — it's like a fingerprint for atoms.
student_glossary.example: Sodium always produces a bright yellow flame and the same pattern of spectral lines — because sodium's electrons always jump between the same energy levels.

sub_terms.definition: A simple lab test where you hold a sample in a flame and identify the element by the colour it produces — sodium gives yellow, copper gives green, lithium gives red.
When an electron jumps from one shell to another. Jumping down releases energy as light — the specific colour depends on the gap between the shells.
sub_terms.example: When a sodium electron drops from a higher shell back to its normal position, it releases exactly the right amount of energy to produce yellow light.

student_glossary.definition: A vertical column in the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons, which is why they behave similarly in chemical reactions.
student_glossary.example: Lithium, sodium and potassium are all in Group 1 — they all have 1 outer electron, so they all react vigorously with water for the same structural reason.

student_glossary.definition: Group 18 elements (like helium, neon, argon) with a full outer shell. They don't react because they have no reason to lose, gain or share electrons — their outer shell is already complete and stable.
student_glossary.example: Neon signs work because neon is so unreactive that it just glows when electricity passes through it — it doesn't react with anything in the tube.

student_glossary.definition: Group 1 elements (like lithium, sodium, potassium) with just 1 outer electron. That single electron is easily lost, which is why they're the most reactive metals — they only need to lose one electron to get a full outer shell.
student_glossary.example: Drop a small piece of sodium in water and it fizzes violently — it reacts so fast because it only needs to lose one electron to become stable.

student_glossary.definition: Group 17 elements (like fluorine, chlorine, bromine) with 7 outer electrons — just one short of a full shell. They're highly reactive because they strongly attract that one extra electron, especially from metals like sodium that are eager to give one up.
student_glossary.example: Chlorine reacts instantly with sodium because chlorine needs 1 electron and sodium wants to lose 1 — they're a perfect match, forming sodium chloride (table salt).

student_glossary.definition: How readily an element undergoes chemical reactions. Reactivity depends on how easily an atom can lose, gain or share outer-shell electrons to get a full outer shell. Elements close to having a full shell (1 electron to lose, or 1 to gain) are the most reactive.
student_glossary.example: Sodium (1 outer electron to lose) and chlorine (1 outer electron to gain) are both highly reactive — put them together and they react instantly to form table salt.

student_glossary.definition: A horizontal row in the periodic table. Each period represents the filling of one electron shell. When a shell is full, the next element starts a new shell and a new period — that's why properties repeat: the outer electron count resets from 1 back to 8 each time.
student_glossary.example: Period 2 goes from lithium (1 outer electron) to neon (8 outer electrons). Period 3 does the same: sodium (1 outer electron) to argon (8 outer electrons). The pattern repeats because a new shell starts filling.

sub_terms.definition: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus — this determines which element it is and where it sits in the periodic table.
How 'metallic' an element is — metals lose electrons easily, conduct electricity and are shiny. Metallic character decreases as you move across a period from left to right.
sub_terms.example: Sodium (far left of Period 3) is a soft, reactive metal; chlorine (far right) is a reactive non-metal gas. The shift happens because outer electrons get harder to lose as you add more.

student_glossary.definition: The chart that organises all known elements by atomic number into groups and periods. At Year 10, the key idea is that the table isn't just a reference card — it's a map of how electrons are arranged. If you know an element's position, you can predict its properties without ever having studied it.
student_glossary.example: If someone tells you 'Element X is in Group 17, Period 3,' you can immediately predict: 7 outer electrons, highly reactive non-metal, gains electrons easily — that's chlorine, and you figured it out from position alone.

student_glossary.definition: A chemical reaction where two or more substances combine to make one new substance. The pattern is simple: multiple inputs, one output.
student_glossary.example: Iron + sulfur → iron sulfide. Two elements go in, one compound comes out — that's synthesis.

student_glossary.definition: A chemical reaction where one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances. It's the reverse pattern of synthesis: one input, multiple outputs. Decomposition usually needs energy (heat or electricity) to get started.
student_glossary.example: When you heat copper carbonate, it breaks down into copper oxide + carbon dioxide gas — one compound in, two substances out.

sub_terms.definition: Decomposition caused by heating — the heat energy breaks chemical bonds in the compound.
Decomposition caused by passing electricity through a liquid compound — the electrical energy splits it into its elements.
sub_terms.example: Passing electricity through water splits it into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas — the two elements that make up water.

student_glossary.definition: A reaction where one element or group swaps places with another. In single displacement, a more reactive element kicks out a less reactive one from a compound. In double displacement, two compounds swap partners to form two new compounds.
student_glossary.example: Drop a zinc strip into copper sulfate solution — the zinc is more reactive, so it displaces the copper: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. The solution changes from blue to colourless as copper leaves.

sub_terms.definition: One element takes the place of another in a compound — but only if the incoming element is more reactive.
Two compounds swap their ions to form two new compounds — like two couples swapping dance partners.
A ranking of metals from most reactive to least reactive. If a metal is higher on the list than the metal in a compound, it can displace it — if it's lower, no reaction happens.
sub_terms.example: Zinc is above copper in the activity series, so zinc can displace copper from copper sulfate. But copper is below zinc, so copper in zinc sulfate would do nothing.

sub_terms.definition: A double displacement reaction between an acid and a base that produces a salt and water. The acid and base 'cancel each other out.'
sub_terms.example: Hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride (table salt) + water. The acid and base neutralise each other.

sub_terms.definition: A double displacement reaction where one of the products is insoluble — it forms a solid (precipitate) that appears when you mix two clear solutions.
sub_terms.example: Mix silver nitrate solution with sodium chloride solution and a white solid (silver chloride) instantly appears — that solid is the precipitate.

sub_terms.definition: The insoluble solid that forms and settles out of a solution during a precipitation reaction.

student_glossary.definition: The idea that for a chemical reaction to happen, particles must collide with each other AND the collision must have enough energy. Not every collision causes a reaction — only the ones that hit hard enough. This one idea explains why all four rate factors work.
student_glossary.example: Imagine a room full of people walking slowly — they rarely bump into each other. Speed everyone up (raise the temperature) and collisions happen more often and harder. That's collision theory in action.

sub_terms.definition: The minimum amount of energy a collision needs to actually start a reaction. Think of it as a hill you have to push the ball over before it can roll down the other side.
sub_terms.example: Striking a match provides the activation energy — the heat from friction starts the reaction, and then it keeps going on its own.

student_glossary.definition: How fast a chemical reaction happens — how quickly reactants turn into products. The same reaction can go fast or slow depending on conditions like temperature and concentration. Rate isn't fixed; it's controllable.
student_glossary.example: An iron nail rusts over months (slow reaction rate), but steel wool in a flame burns in seconds (fast rate) — same reaction (iron + oxygen), very different rates because of surface area and temperature.

sub_terms.definition: Higher temperature = faster particles = more frequent and harder collisions = faster reaction.
sub_terms.example: Food goes off faster in a warm kitchen than in a fridge — the higher temperature speeds up the chemical reactions that cause spoiling.

sub_terms.definition: More particles in the same space = more frequent collisions = faster reaction.
sub_terms.example: Dropping magnesium in concentrated acid produces vigorous fizzing; the same magnesium in dilute acid fizzes much more slowly.

sub_terms.definition: Smaller pieces = more surface exposed = more particles available to collide = faster reaction.
sub_terms.example: A sugar cube dissolves slowly in water, but the same amount of sugar as fine powder dissolves almost instantly — more surface area means more contact with the water.

student_glossary.definition: A substance that makes a reaction faster without being used up itself. It works by giving the reaction an easier pathway that needs less energy — like finding a lower pass through a mountain range instead of climbing over the peak.
student_glossary.example: Hydrogen peroxide slowly decomposes on its own, but add a pinch of manganese dioxide and it fizzes rapidly. The manganese dioxide is still there at the end — it wasn't consumed, it just helped.
